summary.text: The strongest convergent signal in ulcerative colitis mucosa is the neutrophil chemokine axis, led by CXCR2. CXCR2 is up in all eight biopsy cohorts (pooled log2FC [gene=CXCR2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=2.814]), has Open Targets genetic support and has clinical-stage antagonists in other indications, which is why it heads the numeric ranking. The other streams qualify that lead. Neutrophils make almost all of its transcripts in inflamed mucosa (share [gene=CXCR2; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; neutrophil_share_inflamed=0.965]), and only a small change survives composition adjustment ([gene=CXCR2; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_log2fc=0.4409]). Baseline CXCR2 separates ustekinumab non-responders (padj [gene=CXCR2; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.ustekinumab.padj=9.69e-6]) but equally separates placebo non-responders (padj [gene=CXCR2; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.placebo (UNIFI).padj=0.0126]). CXCR2 is therefore a druggable but unproven UC target and, above all, a marker of neutrophil influx and disease severity.

Behind the neutrophil signal, several changes belong to resident tissue cells and survive composition adjustment. The epithelium induces the oxidase DUOX2 (adjusted [gene=DUOX2; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_log2fc=1.3161]). Myeloid cells raise IDO1 (adjusted [gene=IDO1; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_log2fc=0.8505]), and inflammatory fibroblasts raise MMP1 (adjusted [gene=MMP1; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_log2fc=1.2636]) and CHI3L1. At the same time the epithelium loses its metabolic and absorptive programme. HMGCS2 falls in all eight cohorts (pooled [gene=HMGCS2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=-3.838]), and the loss is confirmed at protein level ([gene=HMGCS2; type=proteomics_de; source=DATASET:PROTEOMICS_SCHNIERS2019; contrast=inflamed UC at diagnosis vs healthy colon mucosa; log2_ratio=-3.094]). Unlike the chemokine genes, these candidates point at a specific cell type rather than at cell influx.

Causal genetics and biopsy expression largely point at different genes. The strongest Mendelian randomisation hit is IL12B, an established UC drug target and the positive control of the analysis: higher plasma protein raises UC risk (OR per SD [gene=IL12B; type=mendelian_randomization; source=DATASET:MR_UKBPPP_UC; odds_ratio_per_sd=1.539]). JAK2, the second positive control, has a high Open Targets association ([gene=JAK2; type=open_targets_association; source=Open Targets Platform; score=0.7318]) but only a modest expression change. For CD274 (PD-L1), higher plasma protein lowers UC risk (OR per SD [gene=CD274; type=mendelian_randomization; source=DATASET:MR_UKBPPP_UC; odds_ratio_per_sd=0.595]), so its rise in inflamed mucosa reads as a protective feedback rather than an inhibition target. The most induced chemokine, CXCL8, has no causal support (MR p [gene=CXCL8; type=mendelian_randomization; source=DATASET:MR_UKBPPP_UC; p=0.289]).

At the pathway level, inflamed mucosa activates JAK-STAT, TNFa, NFkB and related pathways consistently across cohorts, and the drugged JAK-STAT and TNF axes act as positive controls. In the treatment cohorts, however, non-response signals mostly track severity rather than drug mechanism. NFkB activity is higher in ustekinumab non-responders (padj [type=response_pathway; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.ustekinumab.padj=0.0000484]) and also in placebo non-responders (padj [type=response_pathway; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.placebo (UNIFI).padj=0.00608]). Baseline IL23A does not predict ustekinumab response (padj [gene=IL23A; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.ustekinumab.padj=0.977]). The leading first-in-class candidates, CHRDL2 (fibroblast) and XKR9 (epithelial), remain hypotheses for experimental validation.

expression.text: Across eight biopsy cohorts the most reproducible increases fall into three groups. The first is neutrophil recruitment and neutrophil effector genes: CXCR2 ([gene=CXCR2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=2.814]), its ligand CXCL8 ([gene=CXCL8; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=3.864]), the calprotectin subunit S100A8 ([gene=S100A8; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=4.77]) and the neutrophil aquaporin AQP9 ([gene=AQP9; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=4.075]). The second is matrix remodelling, with MMP3 ([gene=MMP3; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=4.901]) and CHI3L1 ([gene=CHI3L1; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=4.875]). The third is epithelial antimicrobial and oxidative defence, led by DUOX2 ([gene=DUOX2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=4.412]). The interferon-induced IDO1 ([gene=IDO1; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=3.118]) and PD-L1/CD274 ([gene=CD274; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=1.974]) rise in every cohort as well. All of these are pooled log2 fold changes, UC versus control, from a random-effects meta-analysis. Between-cohort heterogeneity is high, so the direction is more stable than the size.

The strongest decreases describe the loss of the mature absorptive colonocyte and its metabolism. AQP8 has the largest pooled loss ([gene=AQP8; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=-5.246]). It is followed by the tight-junction protein CLDN8 ([gene=CLDN8; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=-4.291]), the ketogenic enzyme HMGCS2 ([gene=HMGCS2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=-3.838]) and the sulfate transporter SLC26A2 ([gene=SLC26A2; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=-3.4952]), all down in every cohort. HMGCS2 makes the ketone body that colonocytes burn for energy, so its loss marks a collapse of epithelial energy metabolism. Together with lost transporters and junction proteins, it marks epithelial dedifferentiation rather than a druggable lesion. These genes are biomarkers of mucosal damage, not targets.

REG1A is the least reproducible of the large changes. Its pooled increase is large ([gene=REG1A; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=4.486]), but only six of the eight cohorts are significant. It is not significant in the Leuven infliximab cohort or in the adult colon cohort, and heterogeneity is very high, so the size is driven by the paediatric rectal cohorts. It is a useful contrast to genes such as CXCR2 and HMGCS2, which change in every cohort.

inflammation.text: Paired biopsies from the same MSCCR patients separate local from diffuse changes. The neutrophil and interferon genes are mainly local to inflamed mucosa. CXCR2 is higher in inflamed than in non-inflamed mucosa of the same patient ([gene=CXCR2; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=inflamed_vs_noninflamed_paired; log2fc=1.6972]) but only mildly raised in non-inflamed mucosa versus controls ([gene=CXCR2; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=noninflamed_vs_control; log2fc=0.6399]). IDO1 behaves the same way: paired ([gene=IDO1; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=inflamed_vs_noninflamed_paired; log2fc=1.6828]), non-inflamed versus control ([gene=IDO1; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=noninflamed_vs_control; log2fc=0.535]). The largest paired differences belong to CHI3L1 ([gene=CHI3L1; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=inflamed_vs_noninflamed_paired; log2fc=2.6182]), DUOX2 ([gene=DUOX2; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=inflamed_vs_noninflamed_paired; log2fc=2.4812]), AQP9 ([gene=AQP9; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=inflamed_vs_noninflamed_paired; log2fc=2.409]) and CXCR1 ([gene=CXCR1; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=inflamed_vs_noninflamed_paired; log2fc=2.1931]). These genes track active inflammation and are natural activity biomarkers.

The epithelial losses are also local. HMGCS2 is essentially unchanged in non-inflamed mucosa compared with controls ([gene=HMGCS2; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=noninflamed_vs_control; log2fc=-0.0649]), so its loss appears only where the mucosa is inflamed. SLC26A2 is clearly lower in inflamed than in non-inflamed mucosa of the same patient ([gene=SLC26A2; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=inflamed_vs_noninflamed_paired; log2fc=-1.955]). None of the leading candidates shows a large change already established in non-inflamed mucosa. Within these data, the dominant signature is a consequence of active inflammation, not a pre-existing field defect.

replication.text: The discovery cohort (MSCCR) reproduces well. CXCR2 is up in inflamed UC versus controls in MSCCR ([gene=CXCR2; type=omics_de; source=DATASET:GSE193677; layer=rna; cohort=GSE193677; contrast=inflamed_vs_control; log2fc=2.5984]) and in the same direction in all four microarray and three RNA-seq replication cohorts. The other leading induced genes (CXCL8, IDO1, MMP1, CHI3L1, DUOX2) and the lost epithelial genes (HMGCS2, SLC26A2, CLDN8) are likewise significant in all eight cohorts. CXCR1 is significant in seven. REG1A is the main exception (six of eight). At protein level, an independent proteomics study confirms MMP3 ([gene=MMP3; type=proteomics_de; source=DATASET:PROTEOMICS_SCHNIERS2019; contrast=inflamed UC at diagnosis vs healthy colon mucosa; log2_ratio=0.806], a much smaller change than at RNA level) and the loss of HMGCS2 ([gene=HMGCS2; type=proteomics_de; source=DATASET:PROTEOMICS_SCHNIERS2019; contrast=inflamed UC at diagnosis vs healthy colon mucosa; log2_ratio=-3.094]). The CHI3L1 protein change is small and was not called significant by the authors. CHI3L1 and CXCR2 also keep their change after adjustment for colon segment, age and sex, so sampling site does not explain them.

literature.text: Published support for the leading candidates is thinner than their ranking suggests. CXCR2 has no verbatim-validated literature relation in the graph. Its support is indirect: Mendelian randomisation, colocalisation and transcriptomic papers that call CXCR1 and CXCR2 potential targets related to neutrophil extracellular traps in UC, and a CXCL5/CXCR2 chemotaxis study. For CXCL8, the literature places the axis with its receptors in UC pathogenesis through PI3K/Akt, MAPK and NF-kappaB signalling, but its diagnostic performance was shown in blood for IBD, not in UC mucosa. AQP9 is reported to come mainly from infiltrating neutrophils and to drive NET formation through JAK2-STAT3-mediated pyroptosis in colitis mice, which agrees with the single-cell attribution below. The only direct intervention evidence is preclinical: one study reports that IDO1 drives M1 macrophage polarisation via ER stress and that an IDO inhibitor ameliorated DSS colitis.

For the remaining candidates, the literature is mostly single-study and bioinformatic. CHI3L1 is reported to promote macrophage pyroptosis via a BCAT1/NF-kappaB axis, with a virtual-screen small molecule binding it. MMP1 transcript correlates with endoscopic and histological activity indices and is modified by mirikizumab. DUOX2 protein is among the most elevated in inflamed biopsies, and S100A9 performs well as a marker of active disease. SLC26A2 loss correlates with Mayo score and PUCAI, and LCN2 is proposed as a marker of UC-associated carcinogenesis. TREM1 activation exacerbates colitis in mice, and a TREM1 biopsy signature is associated with treatment resistance. CD274 appears only as a bioinformatic hub gene validated by immunohistochemistry in one series. Many genes with strong expression or genetic support (CXCR1, FCGR2A, JAK2, INHBA, CXCL5) have no verbatim relation at all, so the literature stream mostly adds plausibility rather than independent confirmation.

external.text: Approved UC target classes behave as positive controls on the genetic side. IL12B, the shared cytokine subunit blocked by ustekinumab, is the strongest plasma pQTL Mendelian randomisation hit. Higher protein raises UC risk (OR per SD [gene=IL12B; type=mendelian_randomization; source=DATASET:MR_UKBPPP_UC; odds_ratio_per_sd=1.539]), the signal colocalises with the IBD GWAS and it replicates in FinnGen and a second UC GWAS, so inhibition is the protective direction. JAK2 has the second-highest Open Targets UC association ([gene=JAK2; type=open_targets_association; source=Open Targets Platform; score=0.7318]) and approved inhibitors, yet no cis-pQTL instrument, so it is not tested by MR. Neither IL12B nor JAK2 is among the top biopsy-expression genes: both are genetics-led targets. For CD274 (PD-L1) the direction is protective. Higher plasma protein lowers risk (OR per SD [gene=CD274; type=mendelian_randomization; source=DATASET:MR_UKBPPP_UC; odds_ratio_per_sd=0.595]), with IBD GWAS colocalisation and FinnGen replication (OR [gene=CD274; type=mendelian_randomization; source=DATASET:MR_UKBPPP_UC; finngen_odds_ratio_per_sd=0.734]). Checkpoint blockade would be expected to worsen UC, and its sensitivity analysis is mixed (Steiger direction correct, Egger intercept null, nominal heterogeneity). CXCL5 also has a protective plasma direction (OR per SD [gene=CXCL5; type=mendelian_randomization; source=DATASET:MR_UKBPPP_UC; odds_ratio_per_sd=0.634]), but without colocalisation. In gut tissue, the strongest eQTL signal (IRF8 in transverse colon, colocalised with the IBD GWAS) does not overlap the top biopsy genes, so blood, gut and expression layers point largely to different genes.

The expression-led candidates lack causal genetic support. CXCR2 has an Open Targets association ([gene=CXCR2; type=open_targets_association; source=Open Targets Platform; score=0.5345]) and clinical-stage antagonists in other indications (reparixin, navarixin, ladarixin, SX-682). It has no cis-pQTL or gut eQTL, so MR is untested, not negative. Mouse colitis papers report that a CXCR2 antagonist ameliorates experimental colitis, but MGI has no curated single-gene colitis phenotype, and no safety events or constraint flags are recorded. CXCL8 has null plasma MR (p [gene=CXCL8; type=mendelian_randomization; source=DATASET:MR_UKBPPP_UC; p=0.289]) and no FinnGen replication. AQP9 ([gene=AQP9; type=expression_meta; source=DATASET:META; layer=rna; log2fc=4.075]) and CHI3L1 have no drug and no genetic association. IDO1 has clinical-stage inhibitors from oncology but no genetic association, and its mouse literature is mixed with no curated MGI direction. FCGR2A combines a high Open Targets genetic score with a modest biopsy increase, a genetics-supported Fc-gamma receptor mechanism that is barely visible in expression. SLC26A3, an epithelial transporter lost in biopsies, has genetic association but no drug.

cells.text: Single-cell data split the leading candidates into neutrophil genes and resident-cell genes. In the dataset that captures neutrophils, neutrophils make almost all inflamed-mucosa transcripts of CXCR2 (share [gene=CXCR2; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; neutrophil_share_inflamed=0.965]), AQP9 ([gene=AQP9; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; neutrophil_share_inflamed=0.92]), S100A8 ([gene=S100A8; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; neutrophil_share_inflamed=0.909]) and CXCL8 ([gene=CXCL8; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; neutrophil_share_inflamed=0.873]). The Smillie atlas did not capture neutrophils and assigns these genes to T/NK or myeloid cells. That disagreement is a capture artefact, not a failed replication. After composition adjustment, CXCL8 is no longer significant (adjusted padj [gene=CXCL8; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_padj=0.0523]), and neither is LCN2 ([gene=LCN2; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_padj=0.206]): their bulk rise is cell influx. CXCR2 ([gene=CXCR2; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_log2fc=0.4409]), AQP9 ([gene=AQP9; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_log2fc=0.8551]) and S100A8 ([gene=S100A8; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_log2fc=0.9231]) shrink but stay significant. The adjustment can over-correct when resident cells become activated, so loss of significance is not proof of pure influx. These neutrophil genes are best read as markers of inflammation; as targets they would act on the infiltrate, not on the tissue.

Four candidates point at resident cells and keep a substantial change after adjustment. DUOX2 is epithelial: enterocytes carry most of its transcripts ([gene=DUOX2; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; dominant_lineage_share=0.947]), replicated in the second dataset. It keeps a strong adjusted change ([gene=DUOX2; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_log2fc=1.3161]), which makes it the cleanest tissue-intrinsic induction. IDO1 is myeloid (macrophages and DC1, both datasets agree), and neutrophils contribute little ([gene=IDO1; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; neutrophil_share_inflamed=0.072]). Its adjusted change stays significant ([gene=IDO1; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_log2fc=0.8505]). CHI3L1 comes mainly from inflammatory fibroblasts ([gene=CHI3L1; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; dominant_lineage_share=0.941]), with a sizeable neutrophil share as well, and keeps an adjusted change ([gene=CHI3L1; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_log2fc=1.3967]). MMP1 also comes from inflammatory fibroblasts, replicated in the second dataset ([gene=MMP1; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_log2fc=1.2636]). These four are the candidates where a drug would act on a defined resident cell.

CD274 has a mixed source. Neutrophils contribute a large share in the neutrophil-capturing dataset ([gene=CD274; type=sc_summary; source=DATASET:SCP259; neutrophil_share_inflamed=0.687]), while the Smillie atlas assigns plasma cells, macrophages and enterocytes, and myeloid dominance replicates. Its adjusted change persists ([gene=CD274; type=composition_effect; source=ANALYSIS:composition; layer=rna; adjusted_log2fc=0.4978]). In situ, the epithelial attribution of DUOX2 is confirmed in Xenium cells and Visium spots. MMP1 is not detected above background on CosMx or Xenium, so its fibroblast attribution rests on dissociated single cells and Visium deconvolution only.

spatial.text: Spatial data were assessed for two leading candidates. For MMP1, inflammatory fibroblasts explain most of the signal in deconvolved Visium spots ([gene=MMP1; type=spatial_visium_cell; source=DATASET:GSE189184; in_situ_contribution=0.579]), which agrees with the dissociated single-cell attribution. MMP1 is not detected above background on the CosMx or Xenium single-cell panels, so tissue spots and single cells agree on the source cell, but the in-situ single-cell confirmation is missing. For DUOX2, the epithelial group is the top in-situ source in both Xenium and Visium, consistent with the enterocyte attribution. The neighbourhood of high-expression spots (which cells surround them) was not reported for the other candidates, so the spatial view does not yet cover the neutrophil genes.

pathways.text: Pathway activity inferred from target genes shows a broad, reproducible inflammatory programme. JAK-STAT activity is raised in inflamed mucosa in all eight cohorts ([type=pathway_activity; source=ANALYSIS:pathways; cohorts_up=8]), which is the most direct link to an already drugged axis. TNFa and NFkB, the anti-TNF axis, are up in every cohort with very high t statistics, and so are EGFR, MAPK, PI3K, TGFb and Hypoxia. Among transcription factors, STAT3 (activity inferred from its targets, consistent with gp130-family cytokine signalling) and AP1 with the ATF/CEBPB family are up in every cohort. Inflamed mucosa activates many pathways at once, so these are broad state markers, not specific targets. As a negative result, p53 activity is not raised: it is significantly lower in only a minority of cohorts ([type=pathway_activity; source=ANALYSIS:pathways; cohorts_down=3]) and non-significant elsewhere.

The most specific cell-cell circuit is neutrophil-to-neutrophil: CXCL8 from CXCR4-high neutrophils acts on CXCR2 on neutrophils, and this circuit is higher in inflamed than uninflamed mucosa (log2 change [type=cell_communication; source=ANALYSIS:communication; log2_change=2.755]). Neutrophil CXCL8 also reaches the atypical receptor ACKR1 on endothelial cells with the highest scores, which fits venular chemokine presentation. The top IL1B circuit runs from monocyte-derived macrophages to neutrophils through IL1R2, a decoy receptor, so it does not imply activating signalling. As a negative result, the neutrophil OSM to fibroblast IL6ST circuit scores low and does not rise in inflamed mucosa (log2 change [type=cell_communication; source=ANALYSIS:communication; log2_change=-0.709]), with no OSMR pair returned. A neutrophil-cytokine-to-inflammatory-fibroblast axis is therefore not supported here. All circuits are ligand-receptor co-expression, which is not proof of signalling.

Separating targeted from untargeted axes: JAK-STAT and TNF are drugged in UC, and IL1B is drugged in other indications (canakinumab). The CXCL8-CXCR2 circuit has clinical-stage antagonists of CXCR1 and CXCR2 (reparixin at late stage) and two anti-CXCL8 antibodies at mid stage, none established in UC. Its transcripts come from infiltrating neutrophils in both the ligand and the receptor cell. TREM1 is up in all eight cohorts but has only a mid-stage peptide (nangibotide) and no ligand-receptor pair passing the thresholds, so it is a not-yet-targeted myeloid candidate without an assigned circuit. DUOX2, CHI3L1 and AQP9 are consistently up with no drug and no genetic support. The IL23A/IL12B and integrin axes were not queried for circuits in this pass.

treatment.text: In baseline biopsies, the leading neutrophil and myeloid genes are associated with non-response, but mostly as markers of severity. Higher CXCR2 is associated with ustekinumab non-response (BH padj [gene=CXCR2; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.ustekinumab.padj=9.69e-6]), yet the drug-versus-placebo interaction is null (padj [gene=CXCR2; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; interaction.ustekinumab.padj=0.982]). The same holds for CXCL8, significant in the ustekinumab arm (padj [gene=CXCL8; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.ustekinumab.padj=0.000102]) and in UNIFI placebo (padj [gene=CXCL8; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.placebo (UNIFI).padj=0.0154]). TREM1 behaves likewise: ustekinumab (padj [gene=TREM1; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.ustekinumab.padj=0.0000474]), placebo (padj [gene=TREM1; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.placebo (UNIFI).padj=0.0234]). OSM is significant in the ustekinumab arm (padj [gene=OSM; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.ustekinumab.padj=0.0000264]) but not in UNIFI placebo (padj [gene=OSM; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.placebo (UNIFI).padj=0.116]). Its interaction is not significant and golimumab shows nothing (padj [gene=OSM; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.golimumab.padj=0.994]), so evidence for a drug-specific OSM effect is weak. Baseline IL23A, in the ustekinumab target pathway, does not predict ustekinumab response (padj [gene=IL23A; type=treatment_response; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.ustekinumab.padj=0.977]). In a small adalimumab single-cell cohort, CXCL8 shows no baseline difference between remission groups and falls in cycling mononuclear phagocytes after treatment (padj [gene=CXCL8; type=antitnf_singlecell; source=DATASET:GSE282122; after_vs_before_treatment.1.padj=0.0253]).

Pathway activity tells the same story. NFkB activity is higher in ustekinumab non-responders (padj [type=response_pathway; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.ustekinumab.padj=0.0000484]) and in UNIFI placebo non-responders (padj [type=response_pathway; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.placebo (UNIFI).padj=0.00608]), and in the PROTECT corticosteroid arm (padj [type=response_pathway; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.corticosteroids (PROTECT).padj=0.00174]). The PROTECT mesalazine arm shows no difference (padj [type=response_pathway; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.5-ASA (PROTECT).padj=0.414]). TNFa activity is higher in infliximab non-responders in one cohort (padj [type=response_pathway; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.infliximab.padj=0.000294]) but does not replicate in ACT1 (padj [type=response_pathway; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.infliximab (ACT1).padj=0.23]) and is raised in other arms too, so it is not anti-TNF-specific. JAK-STAT (ustekinumab padj [type=response_pathway; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.ustekinumab.padj=0.0124]; vedolizumab padj [type=response_pathway; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.vedolizumab.padj=0.571]) and TGFb (ustekinumab padj [type=response_pathway; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.ustekinumab.padj=0.000493]; golimumab padj [type=response_pathway; source=ANALYSIS:treatment; arms.golimumab.padj=0.348]) are weaker and more arm-restricted, and TGFb is also significant in placebo. Across drugs, baseline biology predicts how inflamed a patient is more than which biologic will work. Arms outside UNIFI are small, so their null results are underpowered rather than evidence of absence.

discovery.text: CHRDL2 is the top first-in-class candidate from the discovery screen: up in all eight cohorts and antibody-tractable, with inflammatory fibroblasts as its main source. Two findings temper it. Only a fraction of its bulk signal is retained after composition adjustment ([gene=CHRDL2; type=discovery_profile; source=ANALYSIS:discovery; retained=0.2764]), so much of the rise tracks the expansion of the stromal compartment. Its highest vital-organ RNA ([gene=CHRDL2; type=discovery_profile; source=ANALYSIS:discovery; vital_max_ntpm=42.6]) is the highest among the lead candidates, a safety flag for systemic blockade. What is missing: genetic support, response data, protein and in-situ confirmation, and any functional experiment in fibroblasts.

XKR9 is the only top discovery candidate classed as intrinsic: it is epithelial and keeps most of its change after composition adjustment ([gene=XKR9; type=discovery_profile; source=ANALYSIS:discovery; retained=0.7976]). The weakness is replication. It is up in only [gene=XKR9; type=discovery_profile; source=ANALYSIS:discovery; cohorts_up=4] cohorts, and single-cell expression is sparse, with plasma cells as the top inflamed cluster share, which contradicts a clean epithelial attribution. XKR9 is a hypothesis to test first by targeted replication and in-situ staining, before any tractability work.

LAX1 is a T/NK-lineage, antibody-tractable candidate that is up in all eight cohorts with low vital-organ expression ([gene=LAX1; type=discovery_profile; source=ANALYSIS:discovery; vital_max_ntpm=2.5]), a favourable safety profile. Its composition retention is low ([gene=LAX1; type=discovery_profile; source=ANALYSIS:discovery; retained=0.23]), so most of the increase reflects lymphocyte infiltration rather than a change within T cells, and no response data link it to a drug. It is the weakest of the three as a tissue target but may be useful as a lymphocyte-activity marker.

integration.text: The streams agree on several points. Expression, paired biopsies, single cells, pathway circuits and treatment response all identify the CXCL8-CXCR2 neutrophil axis as the dominant, reproducible and local feature of inflamed UC mucosa. They also agree that it is a neutrophil infiltrate signal that tracks severity, including in placebo arms, rather than a drug-specific mechanism. Expression, composition adjustment, proteomics and in-situ data agree on a smaller set of tissue changes: epithelial DUOX2 induction, HMGCS2 and absorptive-programme loss, myeloid IDO1 and fibroblast MMP1 and CHI3L1. The positive controls behave as expected: JAK-STAT and TNF/NFkB are active in every cohort, and IL12B carries the strongest causal genetic signal.

The streams disagree on causality. The genes with the largest and most reproducible expression changes (CXCL8, AQP9, CHI3L1, DUOX2) have no genetic association, and CXCL8 has a null MR. The genetics-led targets (IL12B, JAK2, FCGR2A) change only modestly in biopsies. For CD274 and CXCL5, higher plasma protein is protective, the opposite of what inhibiting an up-regulated gene would assume. CXCR2 ranks first partly because tractability and Open Targets scores add to its expression, but it has no verbatim literature relation, no MR instrument and no drug-specific response signal. Gut eQTL hits do not overlap the top biopsy genes. The ranking therefore separates three classes: genetics-supported targets, tissue-intrinsic candidates for experimental work, and neutrophil-driven biomarkers of activity and severity.

targets.rationale: Positive control and the strongest causal evidence in the analysis. Higher plasma protein raises UC risk by Mendelian randomisation, the signal colocalises with the IBD GWAS and it replicates in FinnGen, so inhibition is protective. It is the subunit already blocked by ustekinumab. It sits above CXCR2 here, although it ranks lower numerically, because genetics, not biopsy expression, is what supports a causal target.

Positive control: high Open Targets genetic association, approved JAK inhibitors in UC, a modest but consistent expression rise in all eight cohorts, and JAK-STAT pathway activity raised in every cohort. Its rank comes from genetics and tractability, not from the size of its expression change.

Top of the numeric ranking: up in all eight cohorts, local to inflamed mucosa, with Open Targets genetic association and clinical-stage antagonists from other indications. Neutrophils make almost all of its transcripts, little change survives composition adjustment, MR is untested, and its association with ustekinumab non-response is equally present in placebo. It is placed below the genetics-backed controls: a druggable neutrophil-recruitment target to test, and a severity biomarker.

Up in all eight cohorts and local to inflamed mucosa. It is made by resident myeloid cells (macrophages and DC1, with little neutrophil contribution), and its change survives composition adjustment. It has clinical-stage inhibitors from oncology and preclinical evidence that IDO inhibition ameliorates DSS colitis, but no genetic association. Mouse literature is mixed on direction.

The cleanest tissue-intrinsic change: epithelial in dissociated cells, Xenium and Visium, with a strong change after composition adjustment and one of the largest paired inflamed vs non-inflamed differences. It has no drug and no genetic support, so it is listed as a biomarker of epithelial oxidative stress and an exploratory epithelial target.

Inflammatory-fibroblast gene, replicated across single-cell datasets and dominant in deconvolved Visium spots. It survives composition adjustment, is up in all eight cohorts and correlates with disease-activity indices. Broad MMP inhibitors exist but are not validated in UC, and MMP1 is not seen above background on CosMx or Xenium.

Strongly up in all eight cohorts, robust to adjustment for segment, age and sex, from inflammatory fibroblasts (with some neutrophil contribution) and retained after composition adjustment. Preclinical work links it to macrophage pyroptosis. It has no drug or genetic support, and its protein change is small.

Myeloid activating receptor, up in all eight cohorts, with only a mid-stage peptide in other indications. It is associated with ustekinumab non-response but also with placebo non-response, and no ligand-receptor circuit passed the thresholds. It is listed as an untargeted myeloid axis supported by mouse colitis literature.

One of the largest and most reproducible increases, but the bulk rise is cell influx: neutrophil-derived and no longer significant after composition adjustment. Plasma MR is null, and it separates placebo non-responders as well as ustekinumab ones. It is a strong severity and activity biomarker rather than a target, although anti-CXCL8 antibodies exist.

Calprotectin subunit, up in all eight cohorts and mainly neutrophil-derived. It acts as a positive control for the faecal calprotectin biomarker already used clinically. It marks neutrophil influx, not an epithelial change.

The most robust loss: down in all eight cohorts, unchanged in non-inflamed mucosa, lost at protein level and robust to adjustment. It marks the collapse of epithelial energy metabolism in inflamed mucosa; a loss of a metabolic enzyme is not a plausible inhibition target.

Up in all eight cohorts with a mixed neutrophil, myeloid and epithelial source. Plasma MR shows higher protein is protective, colocalised and replicated in FinnGen, so PD-L1 blockade would be expected to worsen UC. It is listed as a protective-axis biomarker, not an inhibition target. The sensitivity analysis is mixed.

Exploratory: the top first-in-class candidate from the discovery screen. It is fibroblast-derived, up in all eight cohorts and antibody-tractable, but only a fraction of its signal survives composition adjustment and its vital-organ RNA is the highest among the leads. It needs genetic, protein and functional validation.

Exploratory: the only intrinsic (epithelial) discovery candidate, keeping most of its change after composition adjustment. It is up in only half the cohorts and has sparse single-cell expression, so replication is the first experiment.

limitations.text: All biopsy evidence is associational. Pathway and transcription-factor activities are inferred from bulk transcriptomes, ligand-receptor circuits are co-expression, and none of them proves signalling or causality.
Composition adjustment can over-correct when resident cells become activated, so loss of significance (CXCL8, LCN2) is not proof of pure cell influx, and retained change is partial for most genes.

Mendelian randomisation uses plasma protein, which is not mucosal protein. Gut eQTL instruments existed for few candidates, and CXCR2 and JAK2 had no instrument, so 'not tested' is not evidence against them.

Treatment cohorts outside UNIFI are small, and non-response in UNIFI is dominated by severity; null arms are underpowered rather than negative. Response was not profiled for CXCL1, DUOX2, IDO1, MMP1, AQP9, CD274 or CHI3L1.

Specialist coverage was budgeted. STRING and UniProt were not queried, the IL23A and integrin axes were not queried for circuits, and spatial neighbourhoods were reported only for MMP1 and DUOX2. CXCR1, CXCL1 and MMP10 were assessed for cell source only through a batch neutrophil-share query.
The literature stream is mostly single-study bioinformatic or murine work, and many leading genes (CXCR1, CXCR2, CD274, FCGR2A, JAK2, INHBA) have no verbatim-validated relation in the graph.

The convergence score adds tractability and Open Targets literature to expression, which favours chemokine genes with drug histories; the target ordering above departs from the numeric ranking for this reason.
